description: We are six people from the IICT institute of HEIG-VD in Yverdon-les-Bains, Switzerland. Yasaman Izadmehr, Simon Walther and Magali Egger turned NASA maps into monthly datasets on one common grid. Teo Ferrari and Léo Zmoos built the composer that turns them into music. Clarisse Estelle Fleurimont built the web jukebox with its 3D globe and put it online. Together we wanted Earth data that anyone can hear, including people who cannot see the maps.
summary:
Earthchestra lets you listen to NASA's Earth maps. You pick a region on a 3D globe and a time period, and eleven Earth datasets are played together like an orchestra, from temperature, rain and sea ice to vegetation, ocean plankton and air pollution. Each dataset gets its own instrument and its own part in the music. We use some rules from music theory so that it sounds good, but the melody, the rhythm and the harmony all come from the data.
To make this work, we first put maps that use different projections onto one common grid, so we can compare their values. Then we write a score from those values and play it in a web jukebox that works with a keyboard and a screen reader. You can also play one month as a vinyl record whose grooves cross the globe, or swap the orchestra for another music style or for the real sounds of rain, fire and thunder.
In Earth science, data are often presented as maps and animations, which blind and low-vision people cannot see. With Earthchestra, they can hear how the planet is changing, and so can anyone who wants to listen and look.
details:
What it does

Earthchestra is a jukebox for Earth data. You choose a place and a time period. The program reads NASA's Earth maps for that place and period and writes a piece of music where each instrument plays one Earth dataset. One frame of the visualization is one bar of music, so what you hear follows what the map shows.

Each dataset and its instrument:

  • Temperature anomaly: piano. Chords, always on: the root follows the temperature, and warmer months play louder.
  • CO₂: contrabass. Bass line, always on.
  • Rain: violins. Melody. Heavy rain becomes a tremolo.
  • Snow: glockenspiel. High melody, struck on every beat.
  • Lightning: timpani. More hits per beat when there is more lightning.
  • Fires: trombones. Swells that grow with the number of fire days in the month.
  • Night lights: synth pad. The only electronic sound. It starts each January, because the data is yearly.
  • Sea ice: bowed glass. A high, sustained line: higher and louder with more of the sea frozen. It thins out every summer, and fades a little more each decade. Silent over land.
  • Vegetation: clarinet. Melody: higher where the land is greener. It rises every spring and falls every autumn; silent over deserts and the sea.
  • Carbon monoxide (air pollution): bassoon. Held swells, louder with more smoke from fires and traffic above the clean background.
  • Ocean plankton (chlorophyll): vibraphone. More strokes per beat in a bloom, on a log scale (each tenfold rise is one step); silent over land.

The tempo follows the world's CO₂ level at each date, so the music speeds up from 1880 to today. An instrument is silent when its dataset is absent from the region or has no data for that month, so an instrument entering is information in itself.

More ways to listen:

  • Realistic mode. Replaces the instruments with the sound of each phenomenon: rain, crackling fire, thunder, creaking ice, crickets for vegetation, engines for air pollution, bubbles for plankton, city traffic that grows louder in warmer months, and for CO₂ a heartbeat that races as the world's CO₂ rises.
  • Music styles. The same notes in eight styles, from a Romantic orchestra through ragtime, swing, rock'n'roll, funk, synth-pop and house to trap.
  • Vinyl mode. One month becomes a record whose 10 grooves of 30 seconds spiral across the globe toward a centre you choose. The needle can travel through places at one date, through time at one place, or through both.
  • Graph and globe. While the music plays, the globe draws the region's values as coloured spots that grow with the data, and a graph shows each dataset month by month.
  • Month travel. One month, year after year: every July from 2000 to today, for example, so you hear how the same season changes over the decades.
  • Key moments. Famous events, such as the Black Summer fires in Australia (2019–20) or the Pakistan floods (2022), jump straight to the right place, date and dataset.

How it works

  1. From map to numbers. NASA maps come in different projections. We put each one on the same 0.25° grid of the globe, one file per month, so we can compare the datasets for any region. CO₂, lightning and night lights are read back from the colours of NASA Scientific Visualization Studio video frames, the same visuals the Earth Information Center shows. Temperature comes from GISTEMP, rain and snow from GPM IMERG, fires, vegetation and ocean plankton from MODIS, air pollution from MOPITT, sea ice from the NSIDC Sea Ice Index.
  2. From numbers to score. For the chosen region, we average each dataset month by month, weighting each cell by its area. Each month becomes one bar of music. Each instrument is scaled on the region's whole history, so the same value always gives the same note, and one 30-second part connects to the next. Everything stays in one key, and each instrument has its own range and rhythm. The tempo of each bar comes from the world's CO₂ record for its date (ice cores, then Mauna Loa), the same for every region.
  3. From score to sound. The server writes the score as MIDI and plays it with sampled instruments (the GeneralUser GS SoundFont; the engine can also use the VSCO 2 CE orchestra recordings) and a hall reverb. No generative AI is used for the music. It is calculated with fixed rules, so the same data always gives the same piece.
  4. The jukebox. The web player streams the music in 30-second parts and plays them back to back. You pick a continent, country, ocean or sea on a 3D globe or in a list, choose the instruments, and jump to any month.

Who it is for

  • Blind and low-vision people, who cannot use the Earth Information Center animations today. The player targets WCAG 2.1 AA: it works with a keyboard alone (Space, arrows, Home/End, M), announces values to screen readers, offers a list instead of the globe, and gives the globe and the graph hidden data tables. It speaks English, French and German.
  • Teachers and museums, who can play a short piece and ask students which instrument is which dataset.
  • Musicians, who can run the engine to get a MIDI score with one track per instrument and make their own music from real Earth data.

What is creative about it

We arranged the data like a real orchestra. Temperature and CO₂, present everywhere, are the foundation: piano chords and bass. Rain and snow carry the melodies, lightning plays the timpani and fires swell in the trombones.

The tempo also comes from the data. It follows the world's CO₂ level, which almost never goes down, so the music keeps speeding up from 1880 to today. In the realistic mode the heartbeat races, from 60 to about 132 beats a minute, and stumbles above 400 ppm.

The styles and the vinyl mode let people come back to the same data and hear it in a new way.

What we thought about

  • If you turn pixels directly into pitches, you get noise. So we keep every note inside one musical scale, and the pitch always follows the data.
  • NASA maps use different projections and colour scales. We wanted the same value to give the same sound anywhere on the globe. Our test put the same NASA layer in two projections on the grid: 98.3% of the cells agreed for rain and 98.4% for fires.
  • People will listen on laptops and phones. Their speakers play almost nothing below about 100 Hz, so the bass plays an octave higher than a real contrabass part.
  • We thought about accessibility from the beginning instead of adding it at the end.

Tools

  • Data: Python, NumPy, pyproj, SciPy, Pillow, OpenCV, xarray.
  • Music: FastAPI, MIDI, VSCO 2 CE orchestral samples, the GeneralUser GS SoundFont with tinysoundfont, FFmpeg.
  • Web: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, react-globe.gl and three.js, i18next, the Web Audio API.
  • Tests and delivery: pytest, Vitest, jest-axe, Docker, Docker Compose, Traefik, GitHub Actions.
  • Use of Super Intelligence (SI): we used SI tools for research, data analysis, coding and debugging, and writing and editing. The team reviewed and tested all SI-assisted code and text. The data values come from NASA and partner sources, and the music is computed from them by fixed rules: no SI model generates the data or the sound.

Links

  • Live app: https://earthchestra.ch/
  • Code: github.com/The-Earth-Information-Jukebox-HEIG-VD: sonification (music engine and API), webapp (the player), datasets (the prepared maps), data_processing (extraction scripts), deployment (Docker)
  • Documentation: the-earth-information-jukebox-heig-vd.github.io/documentation
